but with a stick is the dill knocked out,
and the cumin with a staff.

notes.text: Ephraim, here the northern kingdom of Israel, whose capital Samaria stood on a hill above a fertile valley (about 724 BC). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “the crown of the pride of.”
The mighty one is the king of Assyria. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads Yahweh for ’Adonai (“the Lord”).
Hebrew tsav latsav, tsav latsav, qav laqav, qav laqav, perhaps mocking imitation of the prophet as baby talk, or the letters of the alphabet (tsade, qoph), or “precept upon precept, line upon line.”
Quoted in 1 Corinthians 14:21. The “other tongue” is the Assyrian language.
Sheol, the realm of the dead. “Death” may also refer to the Canaanite god Mot (death).
Quoted with Isaiah 8:14 in Romans 9:33; also Romans 10:11; 1 Peter 2:6. “Shall not hasten,” that is, shall not panic or flee; the Septuagint reads “shall by no means be put to shame.”
Or “to understand the message shall be sheer terror.”
Compare 2 Samuel 5:20 (Baal-perazim, “lord of breaking through”) and Joshua 10:10–14 (Gibeon); there Yahweh fought for Israel, here against it.
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks ’Adonai, reading “from Yahweh of Armies.”
Dill, Hebrew qetsah, black cumin or nigella. Spelt, a hardy kind of wheat. Hebrew “barley in its place,” a word of uncertain meaning (nisman).
Or “Grain for bread is threshed.”
Or “great in success.”

verses.text:
And brought low, you shall speak from the earth,
and your speech shall be low from the dust;
and your voice shall be from the earth like that of a ghost,
and your speech shall chirp from the dust.

From Yahweh of Armies you shall be visited
with thunder and with earthquake and great noise,
with whirlwind and tempest,
and the flame of a devouring fire.

It shall be as when a hungry man dreams,
and behold, he is eating,
and he awakes, and his soul is empty;
or as when a thirsty man dreams,
and behold, he is drinking,
and he awakes, and behold, he is faint,
and his soul is still craving;
so shall the multitude of all the nations be
that fight against Mount Zion.

For you the entire vision has turned into the content of a sealed scroll. If it is given to a person who can read, with the words “Read this, please,” he replies, “I am unable to, since it is sealed.”
And the book is given to one who does not know writing, saying, “Read this, please”; and he says, “I do not know writing.”

And the Lord said:
“Because this people draws near with its mouth,
and with its lips they honor me,
but its heart it has removed far from me,
and their fear of me is a commandment of men learned by rote;{h}

Woe to those who go deep to hide their counsel from Yahweh,
whose deeds are in the dark,
and who say, “Who sees us? And who knows us?”

And in that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book,
and out of gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see.

The humble will find new joy in Yahweh,
and the poorest people will celebrate in the Holy One of Israel.

For the ruthless shall come to nothing, and the scoffer shall cease,
and all who watch for iniquity shall be cut off,

Therefore this is what Yahweh, who ransomed Abraham, says about the house of Jacob:
“Jacob will not be put to shame now,
and his face will not be pale with fear now.

For when he sees his children,
the work of my hands, in his midst,
they shall sanctify my name;
yes, they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob,
and shall stand in awe of the God of Israel.

And those who err in spirit shall come to understanding,
and those who murmur shall learn instruction.”

notes.text: Ariel, a name for Jerusalem, perhaps meaning “altar hearth” (as in Ezekiel 43:15–16) or “lion of God.” Compare 2 Samuel 5:6–9.
Hebrew ka’ari’el, “like an Ariel,” a wordplay: the city shall become a place of burning like an altar.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “with strongholds” (metsodoth). Hebrew “like a circle” (kaddur); the Septuagint reads “like David” (kedawid).
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “your arrogant ones” (zedayikh) for “your foes” (zarayikh, “your strangers”).
Or “her siege works.”
Or “Delay, and be astonished.” Hebrew hitmahmehu utemahu, hishta‘ash‘u washo‘u, a wordplay.
“The prophets” and “the seers” may be explanatory additions.
Quoted, following the Septuagint (“in vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men”), in Matthew 15:8–9; Mark 7:6–7.
Quoted in 1 Corinthians 1:19, following the Septuagint (“I will destroy … I will set aside”).
Compare Romans 9:20–21; 45:9.
Hebrew karmel, “garden land” or “orchard.”
Or “with emptiness” (tohu); “in the gate,” where justice was administered.

verses.text:
“Woe to the rebellious children,” says Yahweh,
“who carry out a plan, but not mine,
and who pour out a libation, but not of my Spirit,
that they may add sin to sin;{a}

who set out to go down to Egypt,
and have not asked my mouth,
to make themselves strong in the strength of Pharaoh,
and to hide in the shade of Egypt!

Therefore the strength of Pharaoh shall turn to your shame,
and the hiding in the shade of Egypt to your confusion.

For his princes are at Zoan,
and his envoys reach Hanes.{b}

They all shall be ashamed
because of a people who cannot profit them,
neither for help nor for profit,
but for shame and also reproach.”

A message about the animals of the Negev.
Through a land of hardship and distress,
where lioness and lion roam, and viper and flying fiery serpent live,
they load their wealth on young donkeys
and their treasures on camels’ humps,
to take to a people who cannot help them.{c}

Now go, write it before them on a tablet,
and inscribe it in a book,
that it may be for the time to come,
a witness forever.{e}

For this is a people of rebellion, sons who lie,
sons who will not hear the law of Yahweh;{f}

leave the way, turn aside from the path,
make the Holy One of Israel cease from before us.”

Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel:
“Because you despise this word,
and trust in oppression and crookedness,
and lean upon them,

so this guilt will be for you
like a crack about to give way,
bulging in a high wall
that collapses all at once, in a moment;

and he will break it as a potter’s jar is broken,
smashed without sparing,
so that there shall not be found among its pieces a potsherd
to carry fire from the hearth,
or to skim water from the pit.”

For thus says the Lord Yahweh, the Holy One of Israel:
“By turning back and by resting you shall be saved;
in being quiet and in confidence shall your might be.”
But you were not willing,

A thousand will run away from the threat of a single one;
you will run away from the threat of five,
until you are left like a pole on a mountaintop,
like a banner on a hill.

Though the Lord has given you bread of hardship
and water of suffering,
your Teacher will no longer hide himself,
but you will see your Teacher with your own eyes.{i}

And when you go to the right hand or to the left,
your ears shall hear a word from behind you, saying,
“This is the way; walk in it.”

And he will give rain for your seed
with which you sow the ground,
and bread, the produce of the ground,
and it shall be rich and plenteous.
In that day your cattle shall graze in a broad pasture;

and the oxen and the young donkeys that till the soil
shall eat salted fodder,
which has been winnowed with shovel and fork.

And upon every high mountain and upon every lofty hill
there shall be channels running with water,
in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall.

And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun,
and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold,
as the light of seven days,
in the day when Yahweh binds up the brokenness of his people,
and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow.

and his breath is like a flooding river
rising to the neck,
to shake the nations in a sieve of ruin,
with a bridle in the jaws of the peoples that leads them astray.

You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept,
and gladness of heart, as when one goes with the flute
to come to the mountain of Yahweh, to the Rock of Israel.

And Yahweh will cause the majesty of his voice to be heard,
and will show the descending blow of his arm,
in furious anger and the flame of a devouring fire,
with cloudburst and storm and hailstones.

For at the voice of Yahweh Assyria shall be shattered,
when he strikes with the rod.

notes.text: Or “who make an alliance” (literally “weave a web”).
Zoan, see 19:11. Hanes, probably Heracleopolis, south of Memphis, or a town in the delta. “His,” perhaps Pharaoh’s, or Judah’s.

The Negev, the dry land south of Judah, through which envoys traveled to Egypt. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “of trouble and dryness and anguish, of lioness and lion, and there is no water.” “Flying fiery serpent,” see 14:29.
Rahab, “arrogance” or “storm,” the name of a chaos monster and a name for Egypt (51:9; Psalm 87:4). Hebrew rahav hem shavet, perhaps “Rahab, they are a do-nothing.”
Or, with some Hebrew vocalizations and ancient versions, “as a witness.”
Hebrew torah, “law” or “teaching.”
Or “Yahweh longs to be gracious to you.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds Yahweh (“Yahweh will surely be gracious”).
Or “your teachers.” The Hebrew moreyka may be singular or plural.
Or “and his burden is heavy.”
Or “with them he will fight in battles of wave offering,” a phrase for brandishing.
Topheth, a place of burning in the Valley of Hinnom where children were sacrificed (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Some read “for Molech” in place of “for the king” (Hebrew lammelek), a wordplay.

verses.text:
How terrible for those who go down to Egypt to get help,
who depend on horses
and put their confidence in the vast number of chariots
and in the great strength of the horsemen,
but never look to the Holy One of Israel
or ask Yahweh for guidance!

Yet he too is wise, and brings disaster,
and does not call back his words,
but will arise against the house of evildoers,
and against the help of those who work iniquity.

And the Egyptians are men, and not God,
and their horses flesh, and not spirit.
When Yahweh stretches out his hand,
the helper shall stumble, and the one helped shall fall,
and they shall all perish together.{a}

For thus Yahweh has said to me:
“As the lion and the young lion roar over their catch,
and though a crowd of herdsmen be summoned against him,
he is not dismayed at their shouting
nor cowed by their noise,
so shall Yahweh of Armies come down
to wage war upon Mount Zion and upon its hill.
Turn back to him against whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted.{c}
For in that day every man shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your own hands have made for you as sin.

And his rock shall pass away in terror,
and his princes shall be dismayed at the banner,”
says Yahweh, whose fire is in Zion,
and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.{e}

notes.text: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “lion” (’aryeh) for “spirit” (ruah) in verse 3, apparently a correction or slip; compare verse 4.
Hebrew pasoah, “passing over,” the verb of the Passover (Exodus 12:13, 23, 27).
Or “from whom you have deeply revolted, O children of Israel.”
Compare 37:36.
“His rock,” perhaps his stronghold, or his king.

verses.text:
Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness,
and princes shall rule with justice.

Each one will be like a shelter from the wind,
a hiding place from the storm,
like channels of water in a parched land,
like the shadow of a massive boulder in a worn-out land.

And the eyes of those who see shall not be closed,
and the ears of those who hear shall give heed.

And the heart of the hasty shall understand knowledge,
and the tongue of the stammerers shall hasten to speak plainly.

The fool shall no more be called noble,
nor shall the scoundrel be said to be generous.{a}

For the fool speaks folly,
and his heart works iniquity,
to practice godlessness,
and to utter error against Yahweh,
to make empty the soul of the hungry,
and to cause the drink of the thirsty to fail.{b}

As for the knave, his tools are evil;
he devises wicked devices
to undo the lowly with words of falsehood,
even when the needy speaks what is right.

But the generous man devises generous things,
and by generous things shall he stand.

Rise up, you women who are at ease, hear my voice;
you complacent daughters, give ear to my speech.

They beat upon their breasts
for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine,

until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high,
and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field,
and the fruitful field is counted as a forest.

Then justice shall dwell in the wilderness,
and righteousness abide in the fruitful field.

And the work of righteousness shall be peace,
and the service of righteousness, quietness and trust forever.

My people will live in a peaceful home,
in secure houses, in quiet places of rest.

Though hail will fall when the forest is cut down,
and the city will be completely leveled,{f}

Blessed are you who sow beside all waters,
who let the foot of the ox and the donkey range free.

notes.text: Hebrew naval, “fool,” the morally senseless man (compare 1 Samuel 25:25, Nabal); kilai, “scoundrel” or “knave.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “his heart devises iniquity.”
Hebrew “Days upon a year.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads the verbs as plural feminine forms and adds “and wail.”
Hebrew ‘ophel, the hill of the city of David (compare 2 Chronicles 27:3).
Or “the forest shall utterly fall.” The Hebrew of verse 19 is uncertain.

verses.text:
At the sound of tumult the peoples flee;
when you lift yourself up, nations are scattered.

Your plunder is gathered like caterpillars gather;
people pounce on it like swarming locusts.

Yahweh is exalted, for he dwells on high;
he has filled Zion with justice and righteousness.

Behold, their heroes cry outside;
the envoys of peace weep bitterly.{d}

And the peoples shall be as burnings of lime,
as thorns cut down, that are burned in the fire.

Hear, you who are far off, what I have done;
and you who are near, know my might.”

The sinners in Zion are afraid;
trembling has seized the godless:
“Who among us can dwell with the devouring fire?
Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?”

Whoever lives justly and speaks honestly,
who refuses to profit from extortion,
who waves away a bribe instead of taking it,
who blocks his ears against plots of bloodshed,
and shuts his eyes against watching evil,

Your eyes shall behold the king in his beauty;
they shall see a land that stretches afar.

The fierce people you shall not see,
a people of speech too deep to perceive,
of a mocking tongue that has no sense to you.

Look at Zion, the city of our festivals!
Your eyes will see Jerusalem,
a peaceful home, a tent that will not be moved,
whose pegs will never be pulled up
and none of whose ropes will snap.

There Yahweh will be our majestic God,
in a place of wide rivers and streams,
where no rowing ship will travel
and no great vessel will sail.

No resident will say, “I am ill”;
the people living there will have their guilt forgiven.

notes.text: Probably Assyria; compare 21:2.
“Their arm,” so the Hebrew; some ancient versions read “our arm.”
Or “Zion’s treasure.”
Hebrew ’er’ellam, of uncertain meaning; perhaps “their Ariel” (compare 29:1) or “I will appear to them.” The Great Isaiah Scroll divides it as ’er’eh lam, “I will see (or appear) to them.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads ‘edim, “witnesses,” for ‘arim, “cities”: “he has despised the witnesses,” perhaps the witnesses to the treaty.

Sharon, the coastal plain; “the desert plain,” Hebrew ha‘aravah, the Arabah, the desert rift south of the Dead Sea; Bashan, the fertile highland east of the Sea of Galilee; Carmel, the wooded ridge by the sea (compare 35:2).
Officials who counted and weighed the tribute and surveyed the defenses. Compare 1 Corinthians 1:20.
Hebrew mehoqeqenu, “our lawgiver” or “our commander.” Compare James 4:12.

verses.text:
Draw near, O nations, to hear,
and give heed, O peoples!
Let the land and its fullness hear,
the world and all its offspring.

And their slain shall be cast out,
and the stench of their corpses shall rise,
and the mountains shall melt with their blood.

The sword of Yahweh is full of blood,
it is gorged with fat,
with the blood of lambs and goats,
with the fat of the kidneys of rams.
For Yahweh has a sacrifice in Bozrah,
and a great slaughter in the land of Edom.{d}

And the wild oxen shall come down with them,
and young bulls with the mighty bulls;
and their land shall be soaked with blood,
and their dust made rich with fat.

For it is Yahweh’s day of vengeance,
a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.

And her streams shall be turned into pitch,
and her dust into brimstone,
and her land shall become burning pitch.

Her nobles, there is none there whom they proclaim king,
and all her princes shall be nothing.

And thorns shall come up in her palaces,
nettles and thistles in her fortresses;
and she shall be a haunt of jackals,
an abode for ostriches.

notes.text: Hebrew heherim, “devoted to destruction” (herem), the ban of holy war.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “And the valleys shall be split, and all the host of heaven shall fall” for “And all the host of heaven shall rot away.” Compare Matthew 24:29; Revelation 6:13–14.
Or “the people of my ban.” Edom, the people descended from Esau, here standing for the hostile nations. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “shall appear” (tera’eh) for “has drunk its fill” (rivvetah).
Bozrah, a chief city of Edom (compare 63:1). Compare Revelation 19:13–15.
Compare Revelation 14:11; 19:3.
Hebrew tohu and bohu, “formlessness” and “emptiness,” as in Genesis 1:2. The identity of several of these creatures is uncertain.
Hebrew lilith, perhaps a nocturnal bird, or the name of a female night demon known from Mesopotamian sources. “Hyenas,” or “howling creatures”; “wild goat,” or “goat-demon” (compare 13:21).
Hebrew qippoz, uncertain, perhaps an owl. Kites, birds of prey.
Hebrew “my mouth.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “his mouth.”

verses.text:
The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad,
and the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus.{a}

It shall blossom abundantly,
and rejoice with joy and singing.
The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it,
the splendor of Carmel and Sharon.
They shall see the glory of Yahweh,
the splendor of our God.

Strengthen the slack hands,
and make firm the tottering knees.{b}

Say to those who are of an anxious heart,
“Be strong, do not fear!
Behold, your God will come with vengeance,
with the recompense of God;
he will come and save you.”

Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened,
and the ears of the deaf unstopped;

then the lame man shall leap like a deer,
and the tongue of the mute shall sing.
For waters shall break forth in the wilderness,
and streams in the desert;{c}

notes.text: Or “like the rose”; Hebrew havatselet, perhaps the crocus or asphodel.
Compare Hebrews 12:12.
Compare Matthew 11:5; Luke 7:22.
Or “the mirage shall become a pool.” Hebrew sharav.
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “and a way.” Or “it shall be for them; the wayfarer, even fools, shall not go astray.”
Compare 51:11.

verses.text: And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah that Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and seized them.{a}

The king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh, his chief officer, with a large army from Lachish to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem. He stopped at the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field.{b}
Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, came out to him, together with Shebna the secretary and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder.{c}
And the Rabshakeh said to them, “Tell Hezekiah, I pray you, ‘So says the great king, the king of Assyria: What trust is this in which you trust?
I say, your counsel and might for war are but a word of the lips. Now upon whom do you rely, that you have rebelled against me?{d}
Behold, you rely on the staff of this crushed reed, upon Egypt, which, if a man leans on it, goes into his hand and pierces it. So is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who rely on him.

But if you say to me, “In Yahweh our God we trust,” is it not he whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah has removed, and has said to Judah and to Jerusalem, “Before this altar you shall bow down”?
Now therefore, make a wager, please, with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to put riders on them.
How then can you turn away even one governor, one of the least of my master’s servants, when you depend on Egypt for chariots and horsemen?
And now, is it without Yahweh that I have come up against this land to destroy it? Yahweh said to me, Go up against this land and destroy it.’”

Then Eliakim, Shebna and Joah said to the chief officer, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it; do not speak in the language of Judah where the people on the wall can hear.”{e}

But the Rabshakeh said, “Is it to your master and to you that my master has sent me to speak these words? Is it not to the men sitting on the wall, doomed with you to eat their own dung and to drink their own urine?”
Then the chief officer stood and shouted in the language of Judah, “Listen to the message of the great king, the king of Assyria!
Thus says the king: ‘Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you.
And do not let Hezekiah make you trust in Yahweh, saying, “Yahweh will surely deliver us; this city shall not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.”’

Pay no heed to Hezekiah; for so says the king of Assyria: ‘Make a blessing with me, and come out to me; and eat every one of his own vine and every one of his own fig tree, and drink every one the waters of his own cistern,{f}
until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards.
Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you, saying, “Yahweh will deliver us.” Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? And have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?{g}
Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their land out of my hand, that Yahweh should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?’”
But they kept silent and answered him not a word; for the king’s command was, “Do not answer him.”

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace manager, together with Shebna the secretary and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah. Their clothes were torn, and they reported the chief officer’s words to him.

notes.text: Chapters 36–39 closely parallel 2 Kings 18:13–20:19. The fourteenth year of Hezekiah, 701 BC. Hezekiah, “Yahweh strengthens”; Sennacherib, king of Assyria 705–681 BC, Akkadian Sin-ahhe-eriba, “(the god) Sin has replaced the brothers.” His own annals record the capture of forty-six walled cities of Judah.

The Rabshakeh, Akkadian rab shaqe, “chief cupbearer,” the title of a high Assyrian official. Lachish, a major fortress city of Judah about 30 miles (48 kilometers) southwest of Jerusalem, whose siege is pictured on Sennacherib’s palace reliefs at Nineveh. The Washer’s Field, see 7:3.
Joah, “Yahweh is brother”; Asaph, “he gathers.” Compare 22:15–22.
Hebrew “I say”; 2 Kings 18:20 and the Great Isaiah Scroll read “You say (you have counsel and might …).”
Aramaic, the international language of diplomacy; Judean, the Hebrew dialect of Judah.
“Make a blessing,” that is, make peace, surrender.
Hamath, Arpad, and Sepharvaim, cities of Syria conquered by Assyria (compare 10:9).

verses.text: And it came to pass, when King Hezekiah heard it, that he tore his garments and covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of Yahweh.
And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz.
They told him, “This is what Hezekiah says: ‘Today is a day of anguish, rebuke and disgrace; it is as when children are ready to be born and there is no strength to deliver them.{a}

Perhaps Yahweh your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, with which his master the king of Assyria sent him to defy the living God, and will rebuke the words that Yahweh your God has heard. Therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left.’”{b}
So the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah.
Isaiah said to them, “Tell your master this: ‘This is what Yahweh says: Do not be afraid of the words you heard, with which the king of Assyria’s servants have insulted me.{c}
Behold, I will put a spirit in him, and he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land; and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.’”
So the Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah; for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish.{d}
Then the king heard a report about Tirhakah king of Cush: “He has marched out to fight you.” When Sennacherib heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah with this message:{e}
“Say this to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Do not let your God, in whom you trust, fool you by saying, “Jerusalem will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.”
Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the lands, devoting them to destruction; and shall you be delivered?
Did the gods of the nations deliver them, the nations which my fathers destroyed, Gozan and Haran and Rezeph, and the children of Eden who were in Telassar?{f}
Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and of Ivvah?’”{g}
Hezekiah took the letter from the messengers and read it. Then he went up to Yahweh’s house and spread it out before Yahweh.
And Hezekiah prayed to Yahweh, saying,
“Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth; you made heaven and earth.{h}
Incline your ear, O Yahweh, and hear; open your eyes, O Yahweh, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to taunt the living God.
Of a truth, O Yahweh, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations and their lands,{i}
and have cast their gods into the fire; for they were no gods, but the work of men’s hands, wood and stone; so they destroyed them.
And now, O Yahweh our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are Yahweh.”{j}
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent a message to Hezekiah: “This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘You have prayed to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria,

so this is the word Yahweh has spoken against him:
“Zion’s virgin daughter
looks down on you with scorn;
Jerusalem’s daughter
shakes her head behind your back.

Whom have you taunted and reviled?
And against whom have you raised your voice,
and lifted up your eyes on high?
Against the Holy One of Israel!

Have you not heard
that I determined it long ago?
From days of old I formed it;
now I have brought it to pass,
that you should be the one to lay waste walled cities
into ruinous heaps,

But I know where you stay,
when you leave and when you arrive,
and how you rage against me.

Because of your raging against me
and because your arrogance has reached my ears,
I will put my hook in your nose
and my bit between your lips,
and I will send you back by the same road
you traveled on.”{n}

This will be the sign for you: this year you will eat what grows on its own, and in the second year what springs up from that; but in the third year, sow and harvest, plant vineyards and eat their fruit.
And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward.
For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and survivors out of Mount Zion. The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will do this.{o}
Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with a shield, nor heap up a siege mound against it.
By the way that he came, by it he shall return, and into this city he shall not come, says Yahweh.
For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.’”
Then the angel of Yahweh went out and struck down 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp; and when people got up early in the morning, there they were—all dead bodies.{p}
Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and went away, and returned and dwelt at Nineveh.{q}

One day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer killed him with the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. His son Esarhaddon became king in his place.{r}

notes.text: That is, the crisis has come, but there is no strength to finish it.
“The remnant that is left,” after the Assyrian conquest of the other cities of Judah. The Great Isaiah Scroll adds, as a correction above the line, “in this city.”
“Young men,” Hebrew na‘are, a contemptuous word for the king’s servants. In the Great Isaiah Scroll, much of verses 4–7 is written as a later correction between the lines.
Libnah, a town of Judah north of Lachish.
Tirhakah, Egyptian Taharqa, a king of the Cushite (Nubian) dynasty that ruled Egypt; he became Pharaoh about 690 BC, but led the Egyptian army as a prince in 701 BC. Cush, see 18:1.
Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, Eden (Bit-Adini), and Telassar, cities and regions in upper Mesopotamia and Syria.
Hena and Ivvah, unidentified cities. The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “and Samaria.”
Cherubim, winged guardian figures above the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–22).
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “and their lands”; compare 2 Kings 19:17.
So 2 Kings 19:19 and the Great Isaiah Scroll, adding “God” (“that you alone are Yahweh God”); the Masoretic Text of Isaiah reads “that you alone are Yahweh.”
Hebrew “the height of its garden land” (karmel).
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “foreign” (“foreign waters”), as in 2 Kings 19:24. “Streams of Egypt,” or “streams of Matsor” (compare 19:6).
So 2 Kings 19:26 (“blighted,” shedephah). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “blighted before the east wind”; the Masoretic Text of Isaiah reads “and a field (shedemah) before the standing grain.”
Compare 30:28.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reverses Zion and Jerusalem. Compare 9:7.
Herodotus (2.141) preserves an Egyptian tradition that the Assyrian army was overrun in a night by field mice that gnawed their bowstrings; compare 2 Kings 19:35.
Nineveh, the Assyrian capital on the Tigris.

Sennacherib was assassinated in 681 BC, about twenty years later. Nisroch, an unidentified god. Ararat, Urartu, the kingdom north of Assyria in modern Armenia. Esarhaddon, king of Assyria 681–669 BC, Akkadian Ashur-ahu-iddina, “Ashur has given a brother.”

verses.text: About that time Hezekiah fell gravely ill. The prophet Isaiah, Amoz’s son, visited him and told him, “Yahweh says: Set your affairs in order, because you will die; you will not get well.”{a}
Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall, and prayed to Yahweh,

and said, “Ah, Yahweh, remember now, I pray, that I have walked before your face in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which was right in your sight.” And Hezekiah wept with great weeping.
Then the word of Yahweh came to Isaiah, saying,
“Go and say to Hezekiah, ‘Thus says Yahweh, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer, I have seen your tears; behold, I am adding fifteen years to your days.
And from the hand of the king of Assyria I will deliver you and this city, and I will defend this city.{b}
And this shall be the sign to you from Yahweh, that Yahweh will do this thing that he has spoken:

Behold, the shadow on the steps, which has gone down with the sun on the steps of Ahaz, I will cause to return backward ten steps.’” So the sun went back ten steps, on the steps where it had gone down.{c}
A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick and had recovered from his sickness:{d}

What can I say? He has spoken to me,
and it is he who has done it.
I shall walk slowly all my years
because of the bitterness of my soul.{j}

For Sheol does not thank you,
and death does not praise you;
those who go down to the pit
cannot hope for your faithfulness.

The living, the living, he shall thank you,
as I do this day;
the father to the children
shall make known your faithfulness.
Now Isaiah had said, “Let them take a cake of figs, and rub it on the boil, that he may recover.”{n}
And Hezekiah had said, “What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of Yahweh?”

notes.text: Compare 2 Kings 20:1–11; 2 Chronicles 32:24. The illness came before the Assyrian invasion was ended (verse 6), probably about 701 BC.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant,” as in 2 Kings 20:6.
Hebrew ma‘aloth, “steps” or “degrees,” perhaps a stairway used as a sundial. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “the steps of the upper chamber of Ahaz” (compare 2 Kings 23:12).
Verses 9–20 are not found in 2 Kings. “A writing,” Hebrew mikhtav; some read miktam, a term in psalm titles (Psalm 16; 56–60).
Or “In the noontide of my days.” Sheol, the realm of the dead.

Yah, a short form of Yahweh; the Hebrew repeats it, “Yah, Yah,” but the Great Isaiah Scroll has it once. “The world” follows a few Hebrew manuscripts (heled); the standard Hebrew text reads hadel, “cessation,” that is, the place where all things cease.
Or “he cuts me off from the thrum,” the threads left on the loom.
Or “I cried out until morning.”
Hebrew ‘arevni, “be surety for me,” stand pledge for my debt.
Or “I shall walk humbly.” The Hebrew of verses 15–16 is uncertain.
Or “by these things” refers to God’s words and deeds.
Or “it was for peace.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll repeats here, in a longer form, words from verse 19, perhaps by a copyist’s error.

Verses 21–22 stand earlier in 2 Kings 20:7–8. In the Great Isaiah Scroll they are written by a later hand in the space after verse 20 and in the margin, which suggests the first copyist’s text lacked them. A cake of figs was used as a poultice.

verses.text: At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah; for he had heard that he had been sick and had recovered.{a}

And Hezekiah was glad because of them, and let them see his house of costly things, the silver and the gold and the spices and the precious oil, and all his house of weapons, and whatever was to be found among his treasures. There was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah left unshown to them.{b}

Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, “What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?” And Hezekiah said, “From a far country they have come to me, from Babylon.”
Isaiah asked, “What did these men look at in your palace?” Hezekiah said, “Everything in my palace was shown to them; none of my treasures remained hidden from them.”
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of Yahweh of Armies:
Behold, days are coming when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have laid up until this day, shall be carried to Babylon; nothing shall be left, says Yahweh.
And some of your sons, who shall come forth from you, whom you shall beget, shall be taken away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”{c}
Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “Good is the word of Yahweh which you have spoken.” For he said to himself, “Surely in my days there shall be peace and truth.”{d}

notes.text: Compare 2 Kings 20:12–19. Merodach-baladan, Akkadian Marduk-apla-iddina, “Marduk has given an heir,” a Chaldean chief who held Babylon against Assyria in 721–710 BC and briefly in 703 BC; he was seeking allies. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and he had lived” for “and had recovered.”
2 Kings 20:13 reads “listened to them.”
Compare Daniel 1:3–7.
Or “peace and stability.”

verses.text:
“Comfort, comfort my people,”
says your God.{a}

“Speak to the heart of Jerusalem,
and call out to her
that her service of war is fulfilled,
that her iniquity is paid off,
that she has received from the hand of Yahweh
double for all her sins.”{b}

A voice says, “Cry out!”
And one said, “What shall I cry?”
“All flesh is grass,
and all its steadfast love is like the flower of the field.{f}

The grass dries up, the flower withers,
but the word of our God shall stand forever.”{h}

Like a shepherd he shall pasture his flock;
in his arm he shall gather the lambs,
and carry them in his bosom,
and gently lead those that give suck.

Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand,
and marked off the heavens with the span,
and held the dust of the earth in a measure,
and weighed the mountains in a scale
and the hills in a balance?{k}

Who has measured the Spirit of Yahweh,
or as his counselor has instructed him?{l}

With whom did he consult, and who gave him understanding,
and taught him in the path of justice,
and taught him knowledge,
and made known to him the way of discernment?

Lebanon would not suffice for fuel,
nor its beasts suffice for a burnt offering.

All the nations are as nothing before him;
they are counted by him as less than nothing and emptiness.{n}

To whom then will you compare God,
or what likeness will you set beside him?

Have you not known? Have you not heard?
Was it not declared to you from the first?
Have you not discerned it since the earth was founded?

who brings rulers to nothing,
and makes the judges of the earth as emptiness.{r}

They are barely planted, barely sown,
their stems have barely put down roots in the ground,
when he blows on them and they wither,
and a whirlwind sweeps them away like straw.

“To whom then will you compare me,
that I should be his equal?” says the Holy One.

Jacob, why do you say,
Israel, why do you speak so:
“My way is hidden from Yahweh,
and my right is passed over by my God”?

Have you not known? Have you not heard?
Yahweh is God of the ages,
who created the far ends of the earth.
He grows neither faint nor weary;
there is no searching out of his understanding.

He gives strength to the weary,
and increases the power of those who have none.{t}

Even youths shall faint and be weary,
and young men shall stumble and fall;

notes.text: Chapters 40–66 address the exiles in Babylon and their return; many scholars assign them to a later prophet or prophets in the tradition of Isaiah (often called Second and Third Isaiah, chapters 40–55 and 56–66), while others hold to the unity of the book. The two halves share many themes, such as “the Holy One of Israel.” The Septuagint adds “O priests” in verse 2.
Or “her hard service.” Hebrew tsava’, “army,” “warfare,” here forced service. “Double” may mean full payment, a full equivalent.
Or “A voice calls out in the wilderness, ‘Make ready the way of Yahweh.’” The Septuagint, followed by Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4, and John 1:23, links “in the wilderness” with the voice.
Luke 3:5 quotes verses 4–5 from the Septuagint.
The Septuagint adds “the salvation of God,” as quoted in Luke 3:6.

“One said”: the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint read “and I said,” making the prophet the speaker. Hebrew hesed, “steadfast love,” “faithfulness”; the Septuagint has “glory,” as quoted in 1 Peter 1:24.

Or “the wind of Yahweh.” In the Great Isaiah Scroll the words from “when the breath” to the end of verse 8 are partly written by a later hand above the line and in the margin; the first copyist’s eye seems to have skipped from the first “the flower withers” to the second. The Septuagint lacks verse 7 and the first line of verse 8.
1 Peter 1:24–25 quotes verses 6–8.
Or “O bearer of good news to Zion … O bearer of good news to Jerusalem.” The Hebrew participle is feminine.
Hebrew Adonai Yahweh. Compare Revelation 22:12.

The span is about 9 inches (about 23 centimeters), from thumb to little finger. “A measure,” Hebrew shalish, “a third,” perhaps a third of an ephah. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “the waters of the sea.”
Or “Who has directed.” The Septuagint reads “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” as quoted in Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16.
Or “like fine dust.”
Hebrew tohu, the word for the formless earth in Genesis 1:2.
The Hebrew of verses 19–20 is uncertain.
Hebrew mesukkan terumah; the meaning is unclear. Some take it as a kind of wood, “mulberry” or “sissoo.”
Hebrew hug, “circle,” the vault or horizon of the earth.
Hebrew tohu.
The “host” are the stars, seen as an army. The Great Isaiah Scroll and some other witnesses read “and not one.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “It is he who gives.”
Or “as the eagle.” The Hebrew nesher may also mean the griffon vulture.

verses.text:
He pursues them and passes on in safety,
by a path his feet have not traveled.{c}

Who has worked and done it,
calling the generations from the beginning?
I, Yahweh, the first,
and with the last, I am he.”{d}

Every man gives help to his fellow,
and to his brother he says, “Take courage!”

The craftsman urges on the goldsmith,
and the one who smooths with a hammer encourages the one who pounds on the anvil,
saying of the welding, “It is good”;
then he fixes the idol with nails so that it will not fall over.

You will look for those who fight you
but will not find them;
those who wage war against you
will be as nothing, as less than nothing.

For I am Yahweh your God,
who grasps your right hand,
who says to you, “Fear not;
I am your helper.”

I will open rivers on the bare heights,
and fountains in the midst of the valleys;
I will make the wilderness a pool of water,
and the dry land springs of water.

that they may see and know,
and consider and understand together,
that the hand of Yahweh has done this,
the Holy One of Israel has created it.

Set forth your case, says Yahweh;
bring forward your strong arguments, says the King of Jacob.

Who told it from the start, so that we could know it,
or from times before, so that we could say, “He is in the right”?
Not one of you foretold it, not one announced it;
not one has heard a word from you.

I first said to Zion, “Behold, here they are!”
and to Jerusalem I give a bearer of good news.{p}

notes.text: “Coastlands,” or “islands,” the far lands of the Mediterranean.
Cyrus II of Persia (verse 25; 44:28; 45:1), who conquered Babylon in 539 BC. Or “whom he calls in righteousness to his service.”
Or “by a path he had not gone with his feet,” that is, so swiftly that his feet hardly touch the road. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “they did not understand” for “he goes.”
Compare 44:6; 48:12; Revelation 1:8, 17; 22:13.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “together” (yahdu) for “tremble” (yeheradu).
Compare 2 Chronicles 20:7; James 2:23. Chapters 41–53 often speak of Yahweh’s “servant”: sometimes Israel, sometimes a figure with a mission to Israel (see the note on 42:1).
Or “my victorious right hand.” Hebrew tsedeq, “righteousness,” often means vindication or victory in these chapters.
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “shall be as nothing and shall perish” and, in verse 12, “You shall seek … not find them,” probably because a copyist’s eye skipped between similar words.

“Redeemer,” Hebrew go’el, the next of kin who buys back a relative’s land or freedom (Leviticus 25:25, 48; Ruth 4:4–6), and who avenges his blood. The phrase first occurs here and is frequent in chapters 41–63.
A heavy board studded underneath with sharp stones or iron, dragged over grain to thresh it.
The identification of several of these trees is uncertain. Hebrew ‘ets shemen, “oil tree,” perhaps the olive or the oleaster.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “or the latter things.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “that we may hear” for “that we may be dismayed and see.”
Hebrew me’apa’, a rare word; many read me’efes, “of nothing” (compare 40:17). The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the word.
Cyrus came from the east (verse 2), and also from the north, after conquering Media and Lydia.
The Hebrew is obscure; literally “First to Zion, Behold, behold them.” The Great Isaiah Scroll differs slightly.
Hebrew ‘awen, “trouble,” “iniquity,” “nothing”; the Great Isaiah Scroll and a few Hebrew manuscripts read ‘ayin, “nothing.” “Emptiness,” Hebrew tohu.

verses.text:
He shall not cry out nor lift up his voice,
nor make it heard in the street;

Thus says God, Yahweh,
the Creator of the heavens, who stretched them forth,
who beat out the earth and all that springs from it,
who grants breath to the people on it,
and spirit to those who walk in it:{d}

to open blind eyes,
to lead out the captive from the dungeon,
and those who sit in darkness from the house of confinement.

Look, the earlier events have happened,
and I announce new ones;
before they begin to appear,
I tell you about them.

Sing to Yahweh a new song,
his praise from the end of the earth,
you who go down to the sea, and all that fills it,
the coastlands and those who dwell in them.{f}

Let them give glory to Yahweh,
and declare his praise in the coastlands.

And I will bring the blind
by a road unknown to them;
by tracks they have never known I will lead them;
I will turn darkness before them into light,
and rough ways into a plain.
These things I will do for them,
and I will not leave them.

They shall be turned back and utterly ashamed,
who trust in carved idols,
who say to molten images,
“You are our gods.”

Hear, you deaf;
and look, you blind, that you may see!

Who is blind but my servant,
or deaf as my messenger whom I send?
Who is blind as the one in covenant with me,
or blind as the servant of Yahweh?{j}

You see many things, but you do not observe;
his ears are open, but he does not hear.{k}

Yahweh delighted, for his justice’ sake,
to make his teaching great and to give it honor.{l}

Which of you will lend an ear to this,
will heed and hear it for days to come?

Who handed Jacob over to the plunderer
and Israel to the looters?
Was it not Yahweh, the one we sinned against,
whose ways they refused to follow
and whose instruction they did not obey?{n}

notes.text: The first of four passages often called the “Servant Songs” (42:1–4 or 1–9; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12). The Septuagint reads “Jacob my servant … Israel my chosen.” Matthew 12:18–21 quotes verses 1–4 of Jesus; compare Matthew 3:17; 17:5.
Or “according to truth.” The Septuagint reads “he shall bring forth judgment to truth”; Matthew 12:20 has “until he brings justice to victory.”
The verbs echo verse 3: he will not burn dim, nor be bruised. Matthew 12:21, following the Septuagint, reads “and in his name the nations will hope.”
Hebrew ha’el Yahweh; the Great Isaiah Scroll appears to read ha’el ha’elohim, “the God, God” (the letter after the first word is uncertain).
Or “a covenant people,” Hebrew berith ‘am, an obscure phrase. Compare 49:6, 8; Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47.
Some propose “let the sea roar” for “you who go down to the sea,” compare Psalm 96:11; 98:7.
Kedar, an Arab tribe of the desert (21:16). Sela, “rock,” perhaps the Edomite stronghold (2 Kings 14:7), or any rocky height.
Or “he triumphs over his enemies.”
Some read “dry land” (tsiyyoth) for “coastlands” (iyyim).
Hebrew meshullam, “one at peace,” “one made whole,” “one dedicated,” or “one repaid”; its sense here is uncertain.
The Hebrew text has “You have seen” (written form) or “Seeing” (read form). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “You have seen many things … they have opened their ears.”
Or “instruction,” Hebrew torah; also in verse 24.
Or “they are all snared by young men,” reading bahurim.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “to plunder” (limshussah, the word of the Hebrew’s written form) without a second “to the spoiler.” The shift from “we” to “they” is in the Hebrew.
Or “the fierceness of his wrath.”

verses.text:
But now thus says Yahweh,
your Creator, O Jacob,
and your Former, O Israel:
Be not afraid, for I have bought you back;
I have called you by name; you belong to me.

Because you are precious in my eyes,
honored, and I love you,
I give men in exchange for you,
and peoples for your life.

I will say to the north, “Give up!”
and to the south, “Do not keep back!
Bring my sons from afar,
and my daughters from the end of the earth,

every one who is called by my name,
whom I created for my glory,
whom I formed, yes, whom I made.”

Lead out the blind people that have eyes,
and the deaf that have ears!

Let all the nations come together
and the peoples gather.
Which of them can announce this
or let us hear about earlier events?

You are my witnesses, declares Yahweh,
and the servant I chose,
so that you may know me, trust me
and understand that I am the same one.
Before me no god was made,
and after me there will be none.{b}

I, I am Yahweh,
and apart from me there is no savior.

Thus says Yahweh,
your Redeemer, Israel’s Holy One:
Because of you I have sent to Babylon,
and I will make all of them flee,
and the Chaldeans in the ships of their shouting.{d}

I am Yahweh, your Holy One,
the Creator of Israel, your King.

This is what Yahweh says,
he who opens a road through the sea
and a path through raging waters,

Do not remember the former things,
nor ponder the things of old.

The wild beasts shall honor me,
the jackals and the ostriches,
for I give waters in the wilderness,
rivers in the desert,
to give drink to my chosen people,

the people I formed for myself
so they would tell of my praise.

Yet you have not called upon me, O Jacob;
but you have grown weary of me, O Israel.

Remind me; let us go to judgment together;
set forth your case, that you may be proved right.

Your first father sinned,
and your spokesmen transgressed against me.{i}

notes.text: Cush, the upper Nile region (Nubia, in modern Sudan). Seba, probably a land near Cush (Genesis 10:7). In the Great Isaiah Scroll “your Redeemer” is written above the line in place of “your Savior.”
Compare John 8:24, 28; 13:19, where Jesus uses “I am he.”
Or “From eternity I am he” or “Since the day was.”
The Hebrew of the last line is uncertain. Another reading is “I will smash all the bolts, and the Chaldeans’ cries will become mourning.”
Compare 2 Corinthians 5:17; Revelation 21:5.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “and you have not done.”
Sweet cane, an aromatic reed used in the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23).
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “any more.”
The “first father” may be Jacob (Hosea 12:2–4). “Spokesmen,” Hebrew melitsim, “interpreters,” “mediators.”
Hebrew herem, the ban of total destruction or devotion to God (Joshua 6:17).

verses.text:
But now hear, O Jacob my servant,
and Israel, whom I have chosen.

Thus says Yahweh, your Maker,
who shaped you in the womb, who will be your help:
Be not afraid, Jacob, my servant,
and you, Jeshurun, my chosen one.{a}

For I will pour water on the thirsty land,
and streams on the dry ground;
I will pour my Spirit upon your seed,
and my blessing on your offspring.

And they shall shoot up like grass amid the waters,
as poplars beside the channels of water.{b}

One shall say, “I am Yahweh’s,”
and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob,
and another shall write on his hand, “Yahweh’s,”
and take as his surname the name of Israel.{c}

Who forms a god or casts an image
that profits nothing?

Thus says Yahweh, your Redeemer,
who formed you from the womb:
I am Yahweh, who makes all things,
who by myself spread the heavens wide,
who beat out the land. Who was with me?{o}

who says to the ocean depth, “Become dry,
and your streams I will parch”;{r}

notes.text: Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel, probably “upright one” (from yashar, “upright”); compare Deuteronomy 32:15; 33:5, 26.
“Amid the waters” follows the Septuagint (“as grass between brooks”); the standard Hebrew text reads “among the grass.”
Or “write on his hand, ‘Belonging to Yahweh,’” as a mark of ownership (compare Ezekiel 9:4; Revelation 7:3).
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Yahweh of Armies is his name.” Compare 41:4; 48:12; Revelation 1:17; 22:13.
The Hebrew of the second half of the verse is uncertain; some emend it to “Who declared long ago what is coming? Let them tell us what lies ahead.”
Compare Deuteronomy 32:4, 31; 1 Samuel 2:2.
Hebrew tohu, “emptiness.”
Or “to sit in a shrine.”
The identification of these trees is uncertain. “Laurel,” Hebrew oren, perhaps a pine or ash.
Or “their eyes are smeared over.”
Hebrew tow‘evah, “abomination,” a term for an idol.
The Hebrew may also mean “you must not forget me.”
Or “you shall not forget me,” following the Septuagint and the Great Isaiah Scroll differs slightly.
Or “and glorifies himself in Israel.”
“Who was with me?” follows the written Hebrew text (mi ‘itti), which the Great Isaiah Scroll shares; the read form (me’itti) means “by myself.”
Or “the boasters.” Hebrew baddim, perhaps “empty talkers,” a term for false prophets.
“His servant” may be the prophet. Some read “his servants” (compare the Septuagint).
Perhaps an allusion to the drying of the Red Sea (51:10), or to Babylon’s river.

Cyrus II (“the Great”), founder of the Persian Empire, who conquered Babylon in 539 BC and in 538 BC allowed the Jews to return and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1–4). Persian Kurush; the meaning of the name is uncertain. He is named here and in 45:1.

verses.text:
Thus says Yahweh to his anointed,
to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped,
to subdue nations before him,
and to loosen the belts of kings,
to open doors before him,
so that gates shall not be shut:{a}

And I will give you the treasures of darkness,
and riches stored in secret places,
that you may know that I am Yahweh,
the God of Israel, who calls you by your name.

Woe to him who contends with his Maker,
a potsherd among the potsherds of the ground!
Shall the clay say to him who shapes it, “What are you making?”
or your handiwork, “He has no hands”?{f}

How terrible for one who says to his father, “What are you fathering?”
or to his mother, “What are you giving birth to?”

I made the earth,
and created man upon it;
my hands spread out the skies,
and all their host I set in command.

I have roused him up in righteousness,
and I will make straight all his ways;
he shall build my city
and set my exiles free,
not for a price nor for a bribe,
says Yahweh of Armies.

Surely you are a God who keeps himself hidden,
the God of Israel, who saves.{i}

They are put to shame and disgraced, all of them;
the makers of idols go off in confusion together.

But Israel is saved by Yahweh
with a salvation for the ages;
you shall not be put to shame nor disgraced
to the ages of eternity.

For this is what Yahweh says,
the creator of the heavens (he is God!),
the maker of the earth who set it firm
(he did not create it to be empty,
but formed it for people to live in):
I am Yahweh, and there is no other.{j}

Come together and approach, all you who survived among the nations!
Those who haul their wooden idols around
and keep praying to a god that cannot rescue
do not know what they are doing.

Declare and bring forward your case;
yes, let them take counsel together!
Who made this heard from ancient times?
Who told it from back then?
Is it not I, Yahweh?
And there is no other god apart from me,
a righteous God and a Savior;
there is none besides me.

Turn to me and be saved,
all the ends of the earth!
For I am God, and there is no other.

In Yahweh all the seed of Israel
shall be justified and shall glory.

notes.text: “His anointed,” Hebrew meshiho, the only place in the Hebrew Bible where a foreign king is called Yahweh’s anointed (compare the kings of Israel, 1 Samuel 24:6; Psalm 2:2). From mashiah, “anointed one,” comes the word Messiah. “Loosen the belts,” literally “open the loins,” that is, disarm.
“The mountains” follows the Great Isaiah Scroll (hararim) and the Septuagint; the standard Hebrew text has hadurim, an obscure word perhaps meaning “swellings” or “rough places.”
Or “surname you.”
Hebrew ra‘, “evil,” here “calamity” or “disaster,” in contrast with shalom, “peace,” “well-being.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Shout, O heavens … who says to the earth, ‘Let salvation blossom’” and lacks the last line.
The Hebrew text is difficult. The Great Isaiah Scroll and some other witnesses differ. Compare Jeremiah 18:6; Romans 9:20–21.
Or “Will you question me about my children, and command me about the work of my hands?” The Hebrew word order is ambiguous.
Cush, see the note on 43:3. The Sabeans, see 43:3 (Seba).
Or “Truly, with you God hides himself.”
Hebrew tohu (see Genesis 1:2).
Hebrew tohu.
Compare Romans 14:11; Philippians 2:10–11.
The Hebrew is uncertain; literally “Only in Yahweh, he said to me, are righteousness and strength.”

verses.text:
Listen to me, house of Jacob,
and all who remain of the house of Israel,
you whom I have carried since your birth,
held since you were in the womb:

To whom will you liken me and make me equal,
and compare me, that we may be alike?

Those who lavish gold from the purse,
and weigh out silver on the scale,
pay a smith to work it into a god;
before it they fall prostrate and adore it.

Remember this and stand firm;
call it back to mind, you rebels.{d}

announcing the end at the start
and, long beforehand, what has not yet happened,
saying, “My plan will stand,
and I will do everything I please,”{e}

Hearken to me, you hard of heart,
who stand far off from righteousness:

notes.text: Bel, “lord,” a title of Marduk, chief god of Babylon. Nebo (Nabu), Marduk’s son, god of writing; his name forms part of Nebuchadnezzar (Nabu-kudurri-usur). Their images were carried in procession at the New Year festival; here they are carted off as plunder.
Or “they could not save the load,” that is, the idols could not save themselves or those carrying them.
Yahweh carries his people (verses 3–4), where the idols must be carried (verses 1, 7).
Hebrew hith’oshashu, an obscure word, perhaps “be men,” “take heart,” or “be ashamed.”
Or “My counsel shall stand.”
Cyrus; compare 41:2, 25. “His counsel” follows the written Hebrew text and the Great Isaiah Scroll; the read form has “my counsel.”
Or “my vindication … my deliverance.”

verses.text:
Your nakedness shall be laid bare,
yes, your shame shall be seen.
I will take vengeance,
and I will spare no man.{c}

Our Redeemer, Yahweh of Armies is his name,
the Holy One of Israel.

Sit in silence, and go into darkness,
O daughter of the Chaldeans;
for no more shall they call you
the mistress of kingdoms.

both of these will hit you
in an instant, on a single day:
the loss of your children and widowhood;
they will come in full force on you,
in spite of your many spells
and the great strength of your charms.

notes.text: Babylon, personified as a royal woman, is to be stripped of rank and become a slave girl.
Grinding at the hand mill was the work of slaves (Exodus 11:5; Judges 16:21).
The Hebrew of the last line is uncertain; literally “I will not meet a man.” Some read “says our Redeemer” with verse 4.
Or “their end,” or “its latter end.” Or “I shall be forever, a mistress forever.”
Compare Revelation 18:7–8.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “in your knowledge” (bedatekh) for “in your wickedness” (bera‘atekh).
Or “which you will not know how to charm away.” Hebrew shaharah may mean “its dawn” or “a charm against it.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the last two lines and has “until this day” instead.
“Those who divide the heavens,” astrologers who mark out the sky into regions. Babylon was famous for astrology.
Or “those you have dealt with.”

verses.text:
Listen to this, house of Jacob,
you who are called by Israel’s name
and who came from Judah’s line,
you who take oaths in Yahweh’s name
and call on the God of Israel,
though not honestly or rightly.{a}

Because I knew that you are hard,
and your neck an iron sinew,
and your forehead bronze,

Because of my name I hold back my wrath,
and because of my praise I rein it in toward you,
so as not to cut you down.

See, I have refined you, though not like silver;
I have tested you in the furnace of suffering.{c}

Listen to me, O Jacob,
and Israel, whom I called:
I am he; I am the first,
and I am also the last.{e}

My hand also laid the foundation of the earth,
and my right hand spread out the heavens;
when I call to them,
they stand forth together.

Gather, all of you, and listen!
Who among them has declared these things?
He whom Yahweh loves shall do his pleasure on Babylon,
and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans.{f}

I, I have spoken; yes, I have called him;
I have brought him, and he shall prosper in his way.

Thus says Yahweh,
your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel:
I am Yahweh your God,
who teaches you for your profit,
who leads you in the way you should go.{h}

your descendants would have been as many as the sand,
and the children born to you as numerous as its grains;
their name would never have been erased
or wiped out from my presence.
There is no peace, says Yahweh, for the wicked.{k}

notes.text: “The waters of Judah,” perhaps meaning Judah as a fountain (compare Psalm 68:26). Some read “from the loins of Judah” (mimme‘e).
Or “I made you hear new things.”

The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “I have tested you” (behantikha) for “I have chosen you” (behartikha), the standard Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “I have rescued you from the furnace.” This rendering follows the scroll.
“It” is the divine name (compare verse 9). The Septuagint reads “because my name is profaned.”
Compare 41:4; 44:6; Revelation 1:17; 22:13.
Or “Yahweh loves him; he shall do his pleasure.” The Great Isaiah Scroll differs: “Yahweh loves me; he shall do my pleasure.”
Or “has sent me with his Spirit.” Hebrew Adonai Yahweh. The speaker may be the prophet or the servant.
Or “for your benefit.”
Compare Jeremiah 50:8; 51:6; Revelation 18:4. The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “send it forth.”
Compare Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11.
Repeated in 57:21. This line closes the first of three sections of nine chapters each in chapters 40–66 (40–48, 49–57, 58–66).

verses.text:
And he said to me, “You are my servant,
Israel, in whom I will show my glory.”{c}

And now Yahweh says,
he who shaped me in the womb to be his servant,
to bring Jacob back to him
and gather Israel to him,
because I am held in honor by Yahweh,
and my God has become my strength:{e}

Thus says Yahweh,
the Redeemer of Israel, his Holy One,
to him whom men scorn, whom the nation loathes,
a slave of those who rule:
“Kings shall behold it and stand up,
and princes shall fall prostrate,
because of Yahweh, who is faithful,
the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you.”{g}

telling the prisoners, “Come out,”
and those in darkness, “Appear.”
They will graze by the roads,
and find pasture on every barren hill;

And I will make all my mountains a road,
and my highways shall be raised up.

Shout for gladness, you heavens, and rejoice, you earth;
let the mountains burst into song!
For Yahweh has comforted his people,
and will have compassion on his afflicted.

But Zion said, “Yahweh has forsaken me;
the Lord has forgotten me.”

Can a woman forget her nursing child,
so as to have no pity on the son of her womb?
Even these may forget,
yet I will not forget you.

Look, I have carved you on the palms of my hands;
your walls are always in front of me.{k}

Your sons hurry back;
those who tore you down and wasted you depart from you.{l}

Look up and look all around;
they are all assembling and coming to you.
As surely as I live, declares Yahweh,
you will wear them all like jewelry
and fasten them on like a bride.

For your waste and your desolate places,
and your land that was ruined,
surely now you shall be too narrow for your inhabitants,
and those who swallowed you shall be far away.

Then you shall say in your heart,
“Who has begotten these for me,
when I was childless and barren,
an exile, and driven about?
And these, who reared them?
See, I was left by myself;
from where, then, are these?”

Shall plunder be seized from a warrior,
or a tyrant’s captive slip away?{o}

For this is what Yahweh says:
Even the prisoners of a warrior will be taken back,
and the loot of a tyrant will be recovered;
I will fight those who fight you,
and I will rescue your children.

I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh,
and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with new wine.
Then all flesh shall know
that I am Yahweh your Savior,
and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.{p}

notes.text: The second “Servant Song” (49:1–6); compare 42:1. Compare Jeremiah 1:5; Galatians 1:15.
Compare Hebrews 4:12; Revelation 1:16.

The servant is named Israel, yet has a mission to Israel (verses 5–6); interpreters have seen in him the ideal Israel, a faithful remnant, the prophet, or the Messiah. One medieval Hebrew manuscript is reported to lack “Israel.”
Hebrew tohu and hevel, “emptiness” and “vapor.” Or “my reward,” “my recompense.”
“To him” follows the read form of the Hebrew and the Great Isaiah Scroll; the written form has “not,” “and Israel is not gathered.” The Great Isaiah Scroll also reads “my help” for “my strength.”
Hebrew netsire, “preserved ones.” Paul and Barnabas quote the end of the verse in Acts 13:47; compare Luke 2:32.
Or “to one whose life is despised.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Thus says the Lord Yahweh, your Redeemer, O Israel.”
2 Corinthians 6:2 quotes the first two lines.
Compare Revelation 7:16–17.

The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “the land of the Syenites” (Seweniyim), that is, Syene, modern Aswan in southern Egypt, where there was a Jewish colony in the Persian period (compare Ezekiel 29:10). The standard Hebrew text has Sinim, otherwise unknown.
Perhaps the plans of the rebuilt city, or a mark like a tattoo.

The Great Isaiah Scroll reads bonayikh, “your builders,” for banayikh, “your sons,” the same consonants with a different vowel, a reading also reflected in some ancient versions; the builders outpace the destroyers. The Septuagint has “you shall soon be built.”
Or “Give me room, that I may dwell.”
Hebrew Adonai Yahweh. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “For thus says Yahweh.”

“A tyrant” follows the Great Isaiah Scroll (‘arits), as in verse 25, and the Syriac and Latin Vulgate; the standard Hebrew text reads tsaddiq, “a righteous one” (perhaps “the captives of the victor”). The Septuagint has “a man taken captive unjustly.”
Hebrew Avir Ya‘aqov, “the Mighty One of Jacob,” compare 1:24; Genesis 49:24.

verses.text:
This is what Yahweh says:
Where is your mother’s certificate of divorce,
by which I dismissed her?
Or which of my creditors
received you as payment from me?
Look, you were sold for your own wrongs,
and your mother was dismissed for your rebellious acts.{a}

Why was there no one when I arrived?
Why did nobody reply when I called?
Is my hand too short to buy you back?
Do I lack the strength to rescue?
With a single rebuke I turn the sea into dry ground
and rivers into desert;
their fish stink for lack of water
and die of thirst.{b}

I clothe the heavens with blackness,
and make sackcloth their covering.

The Lord Yahweh has granted me
a disciple’s tongue,
to know how to hold up the weary
with a word.
Each morning he rouses,
he wakens my ear
to hear as those who are taught.{c}

Who among you fears Yahweh
and listens to his servant’s voice?
Let the person who walks in the dark
with no light at all
put his trust in Yahweh’s name
and rely on his God.{g}

Look, all of you who light fires
and arm yourselves with torches:
go, walk in the glare of your fire
and among the torches you have lit!
This is what you will get from my hand:
you will lie down in torment.

notes.text: Compare Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Jeremiah 3:8; Hosea 2:2. The questions imply that there was no formal divorce and no debt; the exile was due to Israel’s sins, and the bond can be restored.
Compare Exodus 7:18, 21; 14:21.
The third “Servant Song” (50:4–9). Hebrew limmudim, “disciples,” “those who are taught”; compare 8:16. In verses 4, 5, 7, and 9, Hebrew Adonai Yahweh.
Compare Matthew 26:67; 27:30; Mark 14:65. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “I did not turn aside my face.”
Compare Ezekiel 3:8–9; Luke 9:51.
Compare Romans 8:33–34.
The Great Isaiah Scroll has plural forms: “who walk in darkness.”

verses.text:
Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness,
you who seek Yahweh:
look to the rock from which you were hewn,
and to the hollow of the pit from which you were dug.{a}

Listen to me, you who know what is right,
you people who have my instruction in your hearts;
do not be afraid of human scorn
or terrified by their insults.

Awake, awake, put on strength,
O arm of Yahweh!
Awake, as in the ancient days,
the ages long past!
Are you not the one who hewed Rahab apart,
who ran the dragon through?{h}

Was it not you who dried up the sea,
the waters of the great deep,
who made the depths of the sea a way
for the redeemed to pass over?{i}

and to forget Yahweh who made you,
who spread out the sky
and laid the earth’s foundations,
and to live in constant dread all day
of the rage of the oppressor,
who is aiming to destroy?
But where is the oppressor’s rage?

I have placed my words in your mouth
and hidden you in the shade of my hand,
so that I may set up the heavens, lay the earth’s foundations,
and say to Zion, “You are my people.”{n}

Of all the sons she bore,
not one leads her;
of all the sons she raised,
not one grasps her hand.

So hear this now, you afflicted one,
drunken, yet not from wine:

This is what your Lord Yahweh says,
your God, who pleads the case of his people:
Look, I have taken from your hand the cup that made you stagger,
the bowl of my wrath; you will never drink from it again;{r}

notes.text: Abraham and Sarah (verse 2) are the rock and the quarry from which Israel came.
Compare Genesis 12:1–3; Ezekiel 33:24.
Eden, Hebrew ‘eden, “delight” (Genesis 2:8). The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “sorrow and sighing shall flee away,” as in verse 11.
Or “law,” Hebrew torah. Compare 2:3; 42:4.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “his arm shall judge the peoples; the coastlands wait for him, and for his arm they hope.”
Hebrew kemo-ken, perhaps “like gnats” (compare ken, “gnat”) or “in like manner.” Compare Psalm 102:25–26; Hebrews 1:10–12; 2 Peter 3:10.
Compare 50:9.

Rahab, Hebrew rahav, “boisterous one,” “arrogance,” a mythic sea monster and a poetic name for Egypt (30:7; Psalm 87:4; 89:10); not the same name as Rahab of Jericho (Hebrew rahav with a different h). “Sea monster,” Hebrew tannin (27:1).
The Red Sea crossing (Exodus 14:21–22).
Repeated from 35:10.
Compare 40:6–8.
Or “He who is bound,” Hebrew tso‘eh, “one bent over,” perhaps a prisoner in fetters.
Compare Jeremiah 31:35.
Some propose “to stretch out” (lintot) for “to plant” (linto‘a).
Compare Jeremiah 25:15–29; Revelation 14:10; 16:19.
The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint read “who shall comfort you?”
Hebrew te’o, a wild ox or antelope, perhaps the oryx (Deuteronomy 14:5).
Hebrew Adonayikh Yahweh, “your Lord Yahweh.”
Or “Lie down, that we may walk over you.” The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “and your oppressors” after “tormentors.”

verses.text: For thus says Yahweh: “For nothing you were sold, and not with silver shall you be redeemed.”
For thus says the Lord Yahweh: “My people went down into Egypt at the first to sojourn there, and Assyria oppressed them for no cause.{b}

And now, what have I here?” declares Yahweh, “seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Those who rule over them howl,” declares Yahweh, “and continually, all the day long, my name is scorned.{c}
So my people will know my name; on that day they will know that I am the one who is speaking: here I am.”

How lovely upon the mountains
are the feet of the herald of good news,
who makes peace heard, who brings tidings of good,
who makes salvation heard,
who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”{d}

Yahweh has bared his holy arm
before the eyes of all the nations,
and all the ends of the earth shall see
the salvation of our God.

notes.text: “Take your seat”: Hebrew shevi, “sit (enthroned)”; with different vowels, “O captive.” “Loose” follows the read form of the Hebrew; the written form, which the Great Isaiah Scroll shares, has “they have loosed.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Thus says Yahweh,” without “Lord.”
Or “wail,” or “boast.” The Septuagint has “on account of you my name is continually blasphemed among the Gentiles,” which Paul quotes in Romans 2:24.
Romans 10:15 quotes the first two lines; compare Nahum 1:15 (2:1 in Hebrew) and 40:9.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “in compassion” (“when Yahweh returns to Zion in compassion”); compare the Septuagint, “when the Lord shall have mercy upon Zion.”
Paul applies the verse to the church in 2 Corinthians 6:17.
After “the God of Israel” the Great Isaiah Scroll adds “he shall be called the God of all the earth” (compare 54:5).
The fourth “Servant Song” runs from 52:13 to 53:12. Hebrew yaskil, “act with insight,” and so “prosper”; the Septuagint has “shall understand.”
Compare 6:1 and 57:15, where the same pair of words, “lifted up and exalted,” describes Yahweh himself. The Septuagint has “and be glorified exceedingly”; compare Acts 3:13.
So the Masoretic Text and the Great Isaiah Scroll; some ancient versions are reported to read “at him.” In 1QIsa-b the word is lost.

Hebrew mishhat, “disfigurement,” and 1QIsa-b agrees. The Great Isaiah Scroll writes the word with a final yod (mshhty), which some scholars read as mashahti, “I anointed”: “so I anointed his appearance beyond any man.” The Septuagint has “so shall your face be without glory from men.”

Hebrew yazzeh, the verb used of sprinkling blood and water in rites of cleansing (Leviticus 4:6; 16:14; Numbers 19:18). The Septuagint has “so shall many nations wonder at him,” and some render “startle.”
Romans 15:21 quotes the last two lines from the Septuagint.

verses.text:
Who has believed what we have heard?{a}
And the arm of Yahweh, to whom has it been revealed?{b}

notes.text: Or “our report,” “our message.” John 12:38 and Romans 10:16 quote this line.
For “the arm of Yahweh,” compare 51:9; 52:10.
Hebrew yoneq, “a suckling,” used of a shoot from a root; compare 11:1. The Septuagint has “we brought a report as of a child before him.”
Or “rejected by men”; Hebrew hadal ishim, perhaps “lacking men,” that is, deserted, or “least of men.”
Hebrew holi, “sickness” (also verse 4), and makh’ovot, “pains.”
Matthew 8:17 quotes the first two lines of Jesus’ healings. The Septuagint has “he bears our sins, and is pained for us.” First Peter 2:24 draws on verses 4–5 and 12.
Hebrew meholal, “pierced” or “wounded”; the Septuagint has “wounded.”
Hebrew musar shelomenu, “the discipline of our peace.”
Hebrew havurah, “stripe,” “welt.” Quoted in 1 Peter 2:24.
Hebrew hifgia‘, “caused to strike,” “caused to meet”; the same verb is rendered “intercedes” in verse 12. Compare 1 Peter 2:25.
Or “and he was afflicted.”
Acts 8:32–33 quotes verses 7–8 from the Septuagint: this is the passage the Ethiopian official was reading when Philip met him. Compare Jeremiah 11:19; Matthew 26:63; 1 Peter 2:23.

Hebrew me‘otser umimmishpat, “from detention and from judgment”; or “without restraint and without justice.” The Septuagint has “in his humiliation his judgment was taken away,” as quoted in Acts 8:33.
Or “who could tell of his descendants?” or “who gave thought to his fate?” The Septuagint has “who shall declare his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”

Hebrew nega‘ lamo, “a blow to them” (or “to him”). For “my people” the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “his people” (‘ammo), and 1QIsa-b appears to read the same, though the final letter there is uncertain. The Septuagint has “because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death.”
Hebrew “he gave,” that is, “one made”; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “they gave.” The Septuagint has “I will give the wicked for his burial.”

Hebrew bemotav, “in his deaths,” a plural perhaps of intensity. The Great Isaiah Scroll writes bwmtw, which some scholars take as “his burial mound” or “his high place.” Compare Matthew 27:57–60, where Joseph of Arimathea, “a rich man,” buries Jesus.
First Peter 2:22 quotes the last two lines, with “sin” for “violence.”

Hebrew hehli, “he made sick.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads wayhalleluhu, which has been taken as “and he pierced him” (compare meholal, verse 5). The Septuagint has “the Lord also is pleased to purge him from his stroke.”
Or “if you make his soul a guilt offering”; the Hebrew verb can be “you make” or “she (his soul) makes.” Hebrew asham, the guilt offering of Leviticus 5:14–6:7.

“Light” follows the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) and 1QIsa-b, both of which read yir’eh ’or, “he shall see light,” and the Septuagint, “to show him light.” A third Qumran copy, 4QIsa-d, is reported to read “light” as well. The Masoretic Text lacks the word: “he shall see, he shall be satisfied.”
Or “by knowledge of him,” or “by his humiliation.”
So the Masoretic Text and, as far as legible, 1QIsa-b; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “his servant.” The Septuagint has “to justify the just one who serves many well.”
Or “with the great.” The Septuagint has “he shall inherit many.”
Or “and he shall divide the mighty as spoil.”
Jesus quotes this line of himself in Luke 22:37; some manuscripts of Mark 15:28 apply it to the crucifixion between two criminals.

Hebrew yafgia‘, “he makes intercession” (see the note on verse 6). The Great Isaiah Scroll and 1QIsa-b read “for their transgressions”; the Septuagint has “and was delivered because of their iniquities.”

verses.text:
For to the right hand and to the left you shall break out,
and your offspring shall dispossess nations
and make desolate cities to be inhabited.

For as a wife forsaken and grieved in spirit Yahweh has called you,
and as a wife of youth when she is rejected,” says your God.

“For a little moment I abandoned you,
yet in great mercies I will gather you in.

In a surge of anger{c} I hid my face from you for a moment,
but with everlasting loyal love I will have mercy on you,”
says Yahweh, your Redeemer.

“This is like the days of Noah to me:{d}
just as I promised that the waters of Noah
would never again flood the earth,
so I promise that I will not be angry with you
or scold you.

Though mountains may move
and hills be shaken,
my loyal love will never leave you,
and the covenant of peace I made will stand,”
says Yahweh, who has mercy on you.

All your sons shall be taught by Yahweh,{h}
and great shall be the peace of your sons.{i}

Should any assail you, it is not my doing;{j}
whoever assails you shall fall on your account.

Look, I am the one who made the blacksmith
who fans the charcoal fire
and forges a weapon for his purpose;
I also made the destroyer who ruins.

No weapon formed against you shall succeed,
and every tongue that rises against you in judgment you shall condemn.{k}
This is the inheritance of the servants of Yahweh,
and their vindication from me,” declares Yahweh.
the Septuagint has “strangers shall come to you by me.”

notes.text: Paul quotes the verse in Galatians 4:27.
Hebrew bo‘alayikh, “your husband,” plural in form (a plural of majesty), like “your Maker.”
Hebrew shetsef qetsef, a play on sound, “a gush of fury.”
Or, with the Hebrew letters divided differently (kime for ki me), “as the days of Noah”; the Great Isaiah Scroll appears to read so, though the letters are uncertain.
Hebrew pukh, the black paint used for the eyes, here a dark mortar that sets off the stones. The Septuagint has “carbuncle.”
Or “lapis lazuli.” Compare Revelation 21:18–21.
The identity of these stones (Hebrew kadkod and eqdah) is uncertain.
Jesus quotes this line in John 6:45.
For the second “your sons” (banayikh) the Great Isaiah Scroll has a waw added above the line, giving bonayikh, “your builders”; compare 49:17.
Hebrew gur yagur, “stir up strife,” “attack,” or “sojourn”;
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks this line.

verses.text:
Why do you weigh out silver for what is not bread,
and your labor for that which never satisfies?
Hear me attentively, and eat that which is good,
and let your soul delight itself in fatness.

See, I made him a witness to the peoples,
a prince and commander for the peoples.
